item.title: One capability, four front doors
item.description: A single operation now has to be an HTTP endpoint, an MCP tool, a chat tool, and a sandboxed code-mode capability at once. Generate all four from one declaration or watch them drift, quietly, into a security bug.

item.title: The number carries its own receipt
item.description: An assistant answers business questions in plain English and every number it reports arrives with the exact SQL that produced it. The real boundary is not the prompt telling it to behave, it is a Postgres role that cannot write and cannot cross tenants.

item.title: The only implementation of our budget was named NoBudget
item.description: Our agent budget interface had exactly one implementation, named NoBudget, that never capped anything. The types checked and the guarantee was absent, which is the defect a model author produces at scale, and the reason correctness has to move out of the reviewer and into the grammar.

item.title: Trusting agents with enterprise data
item.description: An execution model for autonomous agents that survives enterprise security review.

item.title: Your async trace tree is lying about who called whom
item.description: In a concurrent model gateway the active span is the wrong parent, so I anchor every span to the server span captured once at request entry.

item.title: How Removing Docker Taught Me That My Tests Were Lying (And So Was I)
item.description: Removing Docker from your test harness changes OS semantics you never declared, and two passing tests went green because of it.

item.title: Treat the model as a cell, not a function call
item.description: Why I model each LLM call in my app as a derived spreadsheet cell that recomputes when its inputs change, and where that model breaks

item.title: The turn outlives the connection
item.description: When the browser tab closed, the old design sent a kill signal to an agent that was halfway through editing a file, and fixing that forced a second question I had been able to ignore, what the system should do when no one is there to answer.

item.title: Your gold set is lying to you
item.description: Reference answers are artifacts with bugs, and they are the only software in the stack that nobody code-reviews.

item.title: Retrieval you can audit
item.description: Document intelligence where every answer carries its provenance.

item.title: The editor is built from the blocks it edits
item.description: Adding a database backend to a block-based editor introduced no new model tools because the apps and the editor are one tree of typed blocks, and the same purity later cost it its founding CRDT

item.title: Fifteen services, one install
item.description: Delivering a fifteen-service data platform into customer Kubernetes environments in one step.

item.title: Streaming an LLM turn is not streaming text
item.description: Reconnecting to a long agent turn corrupted its answers, and the fix was to stop modeling the turn as a character stream and treat it as a structured object that survives the connection.

item.title: Skills don't have to be a vendor feature
item.description: I rebuilt a provider’s native skills feature as request-time compilation so it runs on models with no skills API, and found the one piece that does not survive the translation

item.title: When the spec is too big to generate from
item.description: A subsystem’s OpenAPI spec was so large and self-contradictory that generating a client from it became a runtime liability, so I hand-built the types instead.

item.title: Pointing at code you can't see
item.description: You can point at a button on a live page an agent is driving and it knows where you mean, but most of what an agent does has no screen, and the only way I found to point at invisible work was to give it a visible projection that carries its own address.

item.title: The memory no one reviews
item.description: The agent forgets everything between runs, so I let the harness mine each run and write lessons into the next one’s instructions, and the hole I did not see is that nothing reviews a rule the machine writes for itself.

item.title: Four reviewers, one mind
item.description: I let an AI agent merge to main when a panel of AI reviewers unanimously approves, and the slow realization was that unanimity from one model is not four opinions, it is one opinion read four times.

item.title: Make the agent record proof a human will actually watch
item.description: Autonomous pull requests should fail the build unless they carry an inline-autoplaying screen recording of the feature, because a recording nobody opens is not evidence.

item.title: LLM spend is an attribution problem
item.description: A month of anonymous model spend taught me that cost governance for AI is identity infrastructure, and the discipline that fixes it already has a name.

item.title: What regulation does to architecture
item.description: Years of healthcare engineering taught me that compliance, taken seriously, is a design input that produces better systems.

item.title: Managing engineers who never sleep
item.description: A year of running AI coding agents turned into an accidental management apparatus, written one rule at a time.

item.title: You can't review your way to trusting an autonomous agent. Let prod be the reviewer.
item.description: We had already built two thirds of an autonomous deploy pipeline by hand and the missing piece was a self-reverting canary that quietly moved the moment of trust off code review and onto a metric.

item.title: Inducing the schema instead of supplying it
item.description: The hard part of turning a pile of documents into a database is not filling the tables, it is deciding what the tables should be, and the rule that made mine work is that a column earns its place only by paying for itself across the whole corpus.

item.title: My Self-Improving Agent Improved Itself Right Into a Coma (and How I Woke It Up)
item.description: A loop that waits for failure to recur learns nothing, and dropping to one trace per lesson cures the paralysis while quietly letting wrong lessons walk in the front door

item.title: In an LLM app, the only manipulation feature worth building is pointing
item.description: I built drag-and-drop authoring, watched it break under JSX iteration, and deleted all 520 lines once I noticed the chat panel could already do every move in one sentence.

item.title: Robots that made burgers
item.description: Directing the software for autonomous burger assembly at Momentum Machines.

item.title: Give a model a tool it doesn't have by hiding the agent loop in the gateway
item.description: How I gave a search-less model web search by running the whole agent loop inside one gateway call, and what that opacity costs

item.title: A lockless hash table in a database core
item.description: Inside SAP HANA, where a single data structure tripled parallel query throughput.

item.title: Forbid the edit by making it impossible to land, not by telling people not to
item.description: A CI gate that regenerates generated files from their spec and fails on any drift can never be satisfied by a hand-edit, and the same trick quietly stops working where the generator’s output ends.

item.title: Database lessons for the agent era
item.description: Agent platforms are rediscovering, one incident at a time, what database engines settled decades ago.

item.title: Your Agent Knows Exactly As Much As the Command You Let It Run, and Not One Assertion More
item.description: A build agent’s confidence reaches exactly as far as the command it runs to verify itself and no further, which turns any gap between the local check and the merge gate into a false green it will go on to defend.

item.title: What it takes to let agents touch enterprise data
item.description: Trust in agentic systems is an architecture property, not a model property.

item.title: Getting an agent to follow the rules is a persuasion problem, not a prompting problem
item.description: Agent skill files quietly use the seven principles of human persuasion to more than double an agent’s compliance, which makes them powerful, symmetric, and silently perishable.

item.title: Why your knowledge graph isn't helping your RAG
item.description: We nearly published the fashionable verdict that GraphRAG is hype. The audit found something better, the structural reasons the published architectures break on enterprise data.

item.title: Where no becomes yes
item.description: A browser reload once made an agent deny a tool its operator was happy to approve, and that accident is the whole argument, that a fail-closed system enforces a line it cannot draw and someone outside it has to decide where no turns into yes.

item.title: When documents become databases
item.description: Schema discovery is a corpus-statistics problem before it is a modeling problem.

item.title: What you can't add later
item.description: I have deleted three abstractions I was sure I would need, and only one of them actually had to be deleted, which taught me the question to ask before building one is not whether I will need it but what being wrong will cost.

item.title: Your agent thinks fine, it's the shell that's killing you
item.description: An autonomous coding agent’s dominant cost is environmental friction re-paid on every tool call, and writing the workaround into the docs only makes the bill bigger

item.title: The model designs, the code enforces
item.description: In an LLM ingestion pipeline, the model gets the judgment that requires reading the document and nothing else. The surprise is how badly the prompt wants to violate that in both directions.

item.title: Tables are images
item.description: Meaning in a table lives in its geometry, and the architecture that survives a real corpus is a per-table router, not an ideology.

item.title: The physical world does not retry idempotently
item.description: What burger-making robots taught me about agents acting on production data.

item.title: When one line of code becomes five things
item.description: The drag-to-rearrange proof passed seven of seven and meant nothing, because a model that writes your interface turns one expression into a screen full of echoes, and you cannot point at the third echo until you give it a name.

item.title: The Second Account Is a Costume, Not a Boundary
item.description: The claude-box pipeline gives its reviewer agent a separate account, yet the only thing that makes the review independent is a fresh context window that nothing can prove was actually clean.

item.title: Free like a puppy, times fifteen
item.description: A product assembled from open source is not the sum of its components. It is the resolution of their disagreements.

item.title: Forcing the race
item.description: Race conditions are not hard to test. They are untested, because teams accept probabilistic reproduction.

item.title: Evaluating systems that answer in sentences
item.description: Evaluation infrastructure is the difference between a demo and a product.

item.title: Data infrastructure and AI infrastructure are different disciplines
item.description: They optimize for different things, fail in different ways, and the hard problems live at the seam.

item.title: Close enough, and too close
item.description: The same distance that proves synthetic data learned the real distribution is the distance that catches it memorizing a real row, so quality and privacy are not two virtues to balance, they are one ruler with a floor underneath.

item.title: Authorization for answers
item.description: We have learned to secure what agents do. The harder question is what they are allowed to know.

item.title: An answer you cannot audit is worth nothing
item.description: Provenance is a data-model property, not a UI feature, and it cannot be retrofitted.

item.title: About
item.description:
I work at the convergence of data infrastructure and AI, as a founding engineer on an agentic data fabric platform for enterprises with complex operational data estates. My scope runs from API contracts and identity models through agent execution, retrieval, evaluation, and Kubernetes delivery, plus the hiring and the standards that keep all of it coherent.

The arc that got me here is unusual on purpose. I started inside the SAP HANA database core, building lockless data structures and chasing nanoseconds with SIMD and RDMA. Then a robotics startup, directing the software that assembled burgers autonomously. Then a big-data platform at SparklineData that Oracle acquired, and Spark-as-a-Service for Fortune 500 workloads at Oracle itself. Then engineering leadership in healthcare: telehealth at eVisit, health-equity fintech at Soda Health. In between, I founded Lakeshore Labs, an AI agents consultancy serving enterprises across Southeast Asia and the Gulf.
